chapters.title: Chapter 2: How Deals Get Done in India

lessons.title: Swap Ratios Explained: How Your Shares Get Converted

children.text: When GSK Consumer Healthcare merged into Hindustan Unilever in 2020, its shareholders received 4.39 HUL shares for each share they held. When ICICI Ltd merged into ICICI Bank in 2002, its shareholders received half an ICICI Bank share for each share. One ratio sounds generous and the other sounds stingy. Neither impression means anything. A swap ratio is not a reward or a penalty. It is a conversion rate between two share prices, and once you understand how it is built, you can check whether yours is fair.

body.text: A swap ratio converts the value of one company's share into shares of another. It is fixed in the scheme months before your shares convert, so from announcement day the target's share price stops trading on its own story and starts tracking the acquirer's.

children.text: The Core Formula

body.latex: \text{Swap ratio} = \frac{\text{Value per share of the absorbed company}}{\text{Value per share of the surviving company}}
body.caption: The result is the number of surviving company shares issued for each share of the absorbed company. Both values come from the same valuation exercise, on the same date.

children.text: Ratios are usually quoted as whole numbers to avoid long decimals. "42 HDFC Bank shares for every 25 HDFC Ltd shares" is simply 1.68 HDFC Bank shares per HDFC Ltd share. Converting every quoted ratio into shares received per one share held makes deals easy to compare.

body.caption: Real Indian swap ratios, converted to shares received per share held
headers: Surviving company shares per 1 share held

cells: IDFC Ltd into IDFC First Bank (2024)
Vijaya Bank into Bank of Baroda (2019)
Dena Bank into Bank of Baroda (2019)

body.text: A ratio below 1 does not mean you lost money, and a ratio above 1 does not mean you gained. Dena Bank shareholders received only 110 shares per 1,000 because a Dena Bank share was worth far less than a Bank of Baroda share. What matters is whether the value of the shares you receive matches the value of the shares you give up.

children.text: How Valuers Arrive at the Ratio
For a listed company scheme, a registered valuer values both companies using the same approaches, gives each approach a weight and arrives at a
relative value per share

. The three approaches from any valuation course all appear: an income approach such as DCF, a market approach using share prices and peer multiples, and a cost approach using net asset value. The weights are a judgement call, and the valuation report must explain them.

markDefs.definition: The value of one company's share compared with another's. For a swap ratio, absolute accuracy matters less than valuing both companies on a consistent basis.

children.text: Worked Example: Malabar Coatings into Konkan Paints

Unlike the cash deal in Lesson 1.2, suppose these two fictional listed companies now agree to merge through a scheme, with Malabar merging into Konkan. The valuer's report shows the following values per share.

body.caption: Valuer's summary: value per share (₹) and weights

children.text: Swap ratio: ₹214 ÷ ₹490 = 0.4367 Konkan shares per Malabar share. The scheme rounds this to 437 Konkan shares for every 1,000 Malabar shares.

body.title: Convert a Malabar holding
body.prompt: Kavya holds 2,000 Malabar Coatings shares. At 437 Konkan Paints shares for every 1,000 Malabar shares, how many Konkan shares will she receive?

body.title: Change one weight
body.question: A minority shareholder of Malabar argues that net asset value deserves no weight for a paint company. If the valuer moved the 10% cost weight to the market approach (so income 40%, market 60%, cost 0%), what happens to the swap ratio?
options: It rises, because Malabar's market value is closer to Konkan's than its net asset value is
It falls, because the approach being dropped was the one where Malabar looked strongest relative to Konkan
It stays exactly the same, because weights do not affect relative value
It cannot be calculated without a new DCF
body.explanation: New values: Konkan = 0.4 × ₹500 + 0.6 × ₹540 = ₹524. Malabar = 0.4 × ₹210 + 0.6 × ₹230 = ₹222. Ratio = ₹222 ÷ ₹524 = 0.4237, down from 0.4367. Malabar's net asset value was a relatively strong number for it (₹150 against Konkan's ₹200), so removing that weight hurts Malabar shareholders. Small changes in weights shift the ratio, which is why the valuation report deserves a close read.

children.text: Who Owns What After the Merger
The swap ratio also decides how the combined company is split between the two sets of shareholders. Konkan has 20 crore shares outstanding and Malabar has 10 crore.

body.caption: The combined company will have 20 crore + 4.37 crore = 24.37 crore shares.

body.title: Malabar shareholders' stake
body.prompt: After the merger, what percentage of the combined Konkan Paints will former Malabar shareholders own? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 4.37 crore ÷ 24.37 crore × 100 = 17.93%, which rounds to 17.9%. Existing Konkan shareholders keep the remaining 82.1%.

body.title: Ownership of the combined Konkan Paints
What happens when one company already owns shares of the other?

children.text: Cross-holdings are cancelled, not converted. HDFC Ltd owned a large stake in HDFC Bank before their merger. When HDFC Ltd merged in, HDFC Bank could not end up owning its own shares, so those shares were extinguished. HDFC Bank then issued new shares only to HDFC Ltd's own shareholders, at 42 for every 25.

Similarly, if the surviving company holds shares of the absorbed company, no new shares are issued for those. When a parent merges a wholly owned subsidiary into itself, no new shares are issued at all, which is why such mergers leave your holding untouched. Always check the scheme's clause on cross-holdings before calculating post-merger ownership.
The Ratio Is Fixed, the Prices Are Not

The valuation date is fixed before board approval, but shares convert only after the NCLT sanctions the scheme, often a year later. Market prices move all that time, while the ratio stays locked. Only a bonus issue, split or similar corporate action by either company adjusts it. That creates an
implied value
for the absorbed company's share, based on the surviving company's live price.

markDefs.definition: What one share of the absorbed company is worth if converted today: the swap ratio multiplied by the surviving company's current share price.

body.latex: \text{Implied value per share} = \text{Swap ratio} \times \text{Surviving company's share price}
body.caption: The gap between the absorbed company's actual price and this implied value is the arbitrage spread, covered in Lesson 3.2.

body.title: Implied value of an HDFC Ltd share
body.prompt: Suppose HDFC Bank traded at ₹1,600 while the merger was pending. At 42 HDFC Bank shares for every 25 HDFC Ltd shares, what was one HDFC Ltd share implicitly worth, in rupees?
body.explanation: Implied value = 42 ÷ 25 × ₹1,600 = 1.68 × ₹1,600 = ₹2,688. If HDFC Ltd traded well below that, the market was pricing in delay, the time value of money or some risk that the merger might not complete.

body.title: After the announcement, Malabar trades in step with Konkan

body.text: Once a share swap is announced, holding the target is effectively holding the acquirer at a small discount. If Konkan falls 10%, Malabar should fall about 10% too, regardless of how well Malabar's own business is doing. If you do not want exposure to the surviving company, the swap ratio is telling you to reconsider your position well before the record date.

body.title: Paid in shares vs paid in cash

columns.label: Share swap
points: You receive a fixed number of the surviving company's shares
The rupee value you receive moves with the surviving company's price until conversion
You share in future gains or losses of the combined company
No cash changes hands, apart from payouts for fractional entitlements
Typical of mergers under a scheme

columns.label: Cash consideration
points: You receive a fixed rupee price per share
The value is locked, regardless of the buyer's share price
You exit completely and have no stake in what happens next
A sale for tax purposes, triggering capital gains
Typical of open offers, delistings and buyouts

body.title: What stays locked
body.textWithBlank: Once the scheme fixes the swap ratio, it does not change when the share ___ of either company move, unless there is a corporate action such as a bonus issue or split.
body.explanation: The ratio is a contract term, not a live market rate. Price movements change the implied value you receive, not the number of shares.

body.title: A ratio that looks too low
body.scenario: A fictional listed parent, Vindhya Holdings, announces it will absorb its listed subsidiary, Vindhya Cables. On the day before the board meeting, Vindhya Cables closed at ₹300 and Vindhya Holdings at ₹1,000. The swap ratio is 25 Vindhya Holdings shares for every 100 Vindhya Cables shares. Vindhya Cables shareholders on social media are furious.
body.prompt: Is their anger justified? What would you check in the scheme documents?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Implied value: 25 ÷ 100 × ₹1,000 = ₹250 per Vindhya Cables share, about 17% below its last closing price of ₹300. Cables shareholders are being asked to accept less than the market valued their shares at.
2. That is not automatically unfair. Market prices can be inflated, for instance by low free float in the subsidiary. Read the valuation report to see what weight went to market price versus DCF and net asset value, and why.
3. Check the valuation date and whether Cables' price had run up sharply just before it.
4. Read the independent directors' report of Vindhya Cables and the fairness opinion for how they justify a ratio below market value.
5. Check the vote rules. Because the parent is a promoter-group entity, the public shareholder majority condition from Lesson 2.1 is likely to apply, so public shareholders of Cables can block the scheme by voting against it.
6. Watch institutional investors and proxy advisors. Their stance often decides whether a contested ratio gets revised.

body.title: Checking any swap ratio
steps: Convert the ratio into surviving company shares per one share you hold
Calculate the implied value using the surviving company's current price
Compare that with the absorbed company's price before the announcement
Open the valuation report and note the approaches, values per share and weights
Check for cross-holdings and how they are treated
Work out what percentage of the combined company your side will own

body.label: NSE India: Corporate Filings
body.description: Search a company on NSE and open its corporate filings to find the draft scheme, valuation report and fairness opinion filed under Regulation 37.

cards.definition: The number of surviving company shares issued for each share of the absorbed company.
Each company's value per share, derived on a consistent basis, used to set the swap ratio.
The average of values from different approaches, each multiplied by the weight the valuer assigns it.
Swap ratio multiplied by the surviving company's current share price.
Shares that one merging company holds in the other. These are cancelled rather than converted.
A share swap gives you a fixed number of shares whose value moves. Cash gives you a fixed rupee amount and a full exit.

points: Swap ratio = value per share of the absorbed company ÷ value per share of the surviving company.
A ratio above or below 1 says nothing about gain or loss. Compare the value you receive with the value you give up.
Valuers combine income, market and cost approaches with weights. Changing the weights changes the ratio, so read the valuation report.
The ratio also sets the ownership split: in the Konkan and Malabar example, Malabar shareholders end up with 17.9% of the combined company.
The ratio is fixed while prices move, so the target's shares trade at an implied value tied to the acquirer's price.
Cross-holdings are cancelled, and mergers of wholly owned subsidiaries issue no new shares.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Konkan Paints, Malabar Coatings, Vindhya Holdings and Vindhya Cables are fictional, as is the ₹1,600 HDFC Bank price used for illustration. Swap ratios for real deals are taken from public disclosures. Always read the actual scheme and valuation report before acting.
